text: Do you like to eat fruit?
I don't eat rice every day.
Have a little of this cake.
Can I have a glass of water?
Do you have time on Tuesday?
On Thursdays we go to the movies.
What do you do on Fridays?
I have lessons in the afternoon.
We watch TV in the evening.
Do you like spring or autumn?

notes: Turkish 'Biletlerin var mı?' asks whether you own tickets of your own; 'Do you have the tickets?' (specific tickets) is 'Biletler sende mi?'.

text: My brother lives in a small village.

notes: 'Giysilerimi seviyor musun?' is a calque; for liking how clothes look Turkish uses 'beğenmek'.
In 'email address' the word email names the system, not 'a message you send over the internet' as glossed.
'Fotoğraf almak' is a calque of 'get a photo'; Turkish says 'fotoğraf çekmek'.

text: It looks like your dog is thirsty.
It's easy to make and it's cheap.

notes: First Turkish translation has a misplaced question particle ('Sağlıklı mı olduğumu sanıyorsun?') and 'sanmak' adds a 'wrongly believe' nuance; unnatural.
In 'sad movies' sad means 'making people unhappy' (üzücü), not 'unhappy' (feeling) as glossed.

text: I'm getting really bored just sitting here.

notes: 'Interesting' is an odd word for a party (natives say 'fun') and often sounds ironic.

text: The exam was too difficult for me.

notes: Turkish 'fotoğraflar çekmektir' uses an unnatural plural; the natural phrase is 'fotoğraf çekmek'.
'Hayvanlarla gerçekten iyiyim' is a calque ('iyiyim' reads as 'I am fine'); 'good with animals' is 'hayvanlarla aram iyi'.

text: I do my homework every day.
Where can I get a ticket?

notes: 'Just' can mean 'a moment ago' or 'simply' (the Tatoeba translations show both), and 'it' needs context.

text: I don't want to go up there.
notes: Turkish 'Oraya gitmek istemiyorum' drops the carrier word 'up'; 'çıkmak' keeps the upward movement.
'Benim sadece zamanım yok' is a calque: 'sadece' (only) misrenders emphatic 'just'.

text: We go to the sea every year.
I have things I need to do.

notes: Incomplete without 'of ...' (first day of what?); only makes sense with missing context.

text: What do you have in your right hand?

notes: Odd as a standalone sentence (which men?); textbook-like.
In the fixed formula 'Nice to meet you' meet means 'get to know someone for the first time' (tanışmak), not 'see and talk to someone by plan or by chance' as glossed.
Turkish 'Oda çok büyük' reads as 'very big'; the carrier 'too' (more than needed) needs 'fazla' or 'gereğinden'.

text: I'm going to call you right back.

notes: Unusual phrasing out of context; natives would say 'Let's call them' or 'Let's give them a call'.

text: I've got something to show you.
I went to see a show today.
Are you still having a good time?

notes: Turkish 'Bu büyük bir dünya' is a calque of the dummy 'it' ('This is a big world'); unnatural.

text: I'm going to need a little help.
Parts of the book are quite good.
notes: Turkish 'Kitabın bölümleri' (the book's chapters) loses 'parts of', i.e. that only some parts are good.

text: I think it's time to go home.
notes: Turkish 'Ben eve gitme zamanı olduğunu düşünüyorum' is stilted translationese.
'change clothes' = take off and put on different clothes (replace sense), not 'become or make different'; Turkish 'Giysileri değiştirmek' reads as exchanging specific clothes.
'have school' means classes / a school day (time in session), not the place where children learn.
Turkish 'Benim büyük ellerim var' is a calque of 'I have big hands'; natural Turkish is 'Ellerim büyük'.

text: I'm going to miss having you around.
notes: Turkish 'Sizi ağırlamayı özleyeceğim' means 'I'll miss hosting you', not having you around.

turkish_fix: Küçük bir erkek kardeşim olsun istiyorum.
notes: 'little brother' means younger brother, not 'small'; Turkish word order 'Bir küçük erkek kardeş' is unnatural.

text: It's bad manners to point at people.
I want to work in a company.
notes: Sounds non-native and vague; natives say 'work for/at a company' and usually name the kind of company.
Usually asks whether someone has a spouse/children of their own; learners may read it as asking about relatives in general.

text: I'd like to ask a question.
I'd like to become a doctor.

notes: 'phone number' is an identifying number (Turkish 'numara'), not a numeral like 1, 2 or 3 ('sayı').
'you guys' is a plural 'you' for any group (any gender), not 'a man'.

text: What are you going to do next?

notes: As a bare command natives would say 'Do it again'; Turkish 'Onu ikinci bir kez yap' is a stilted calque.

text: Let me think for just a second.
notes: 'just a second' means a short moment, not literally one sixtieth of a minute.

turkish_fix: Az önce gerçekten bu mu oldu?
notes: Learners easily read 'just' as 'only' (the Turkish translator did); Turkish 'Bu sadece gerçekten oldu mu?' mistranslates 'just' and is unnatural.

text: Do you want to hold my hand?

notes: Turkish 'Paran var mı?' means 'Do you have (any) money?'; the English asks about specific money ('the money').

text: Do people drink tea in your country?
Many young families live in this area.
Tell me when you'd like to order.

notes: Turkish 'Haklılığına inanıyorum' ('I believe in your rightness') is stilted and shifts the meaning.

text: Draw a line on the paper.

turkish_fix: Bu hafta sonu bir yerlere gidelim.
notes: 'go away' here means take a short trip; learners may read it as 'Go away!' (leave). Turkish 'çekip gidelim' suggests walking out / leaving for good.
'in a month' means one month from now; Turkish 'Bir ay içinde dön' means 'within a month'.
Stiff: in speech people say 'My house isn't very big'; 'large' fits better in contexts like 'a large coffee' or 'a large family'.
Stiff word order; natives say 'It's my turn now' or 'Now it's my turn'.
Odd out of context (states the obvious to the listener). Turkish 'bir saatin var' can also read 'you have one hour'; 'kol saati' would be clearer.
Turkish 'çok fazla çalışmazlar' ('they don't work too much') turns 'hard' (effort) into amount.
Turkish 'Bir sorun var mı?' is read as 'Is there a problem?' (sorun = problem), mistranslating 'question'.
'from the top' is an idiom for 'from the beginning', not the highest part; Turkish 'Üstten başlayalım' takes it literally.
Turkish 'iyi bir kişiyim' is unidiomatic; the set phrase is 'iyi bir insanım'.
Meaning matches the gloss, but 'early' is a predicative adjective here, not an adverb.

text: It's too early for you to come.
notes: Odd without context (come where? too early in the day or too soon?); natives would say e.g. 'It's too early to come over'.

text: What do you think caused the problem?
I didn't know you were a member.
Sit on the other side of the table.
notes: Turkish has a typo: 'tarfına' should be 'tarafına'.
Rather literary/emotional as a standalone line; everyday speech prefers 'I'm very hopeful' or 'I'm full of hope for the future'.

text: We are thinking of moving back home.
You don't seem to be having fun.

notes: Non-native feel: natives say 'I can hear you very well'; bare 'I hear you' usually means 'I understand your point'.
Turkish 'Sadece tam burada bekle' renders the softener 'just' as 'only'; clumsy, unnatural Turkish.

text: The price does not include the box.

notes: Can be literal (carrying things) or idiomatic ('I'm very busy'); the Turkish is a two-sentence paraphrase of the idiom ('I have a lot of work, I can't do another job'), not a translation.

text: This class is too easy for my level.
He's old enough to go to school.
notes: Turkish 'yeterince yaşlı' uses 'yaşlı' (elderly) for a child; calque of 'old enough'.

turkish_fix: Şu an uygun bir zaman değil.
notes: Turkish 'Şimdi kötü bir zaman' is a word-for-word calque; unnatural.

text: Do you want to send a message?
I like that kind of work.
You are much too kind to me.
notes: Formal/dated politeness formula; learners may read 'much too kind' as a complaint (excessively kind). Turkish 'çok fazla naziksin' is literal and stilted.

text: That's not too far away, is it?
We always have to follow the rules.
notes: 'follow the rules' means obey, not 'go behind someone or something'.

text: The cold weather killed the flowers.
I only want to know the facts.
I never actually wanted to do that.
I'm going to take a short break.
I've decided not to continue doing that.

notes: Turkish 'Açık bir zihnim var' is a calque; the natural expression is 'açık fikirli'.

text: I don't mind walking in the rain.
notes: Turkish 'umursamıyorum' means 'I don't care about', not 'it doesn't bother me'; sounds translated.
Comments on a man's physical attractiveness; mildly suggestive and awkward for a couple to practise. A neutral carrier (e.g. about exercise and the body) is better.
'Do you have a minute?' means 'a little time', not literally sixty seconds.

text: I don't think they allow that here.
notes: Turkish 'Onların burada ona izin vereceklerini sanmıyorum' is stilted translationese and shifts to future ('will allow').

text: It really doesn't matter much to me.

notes: Often an accusatory 'What's wrong with you?!' (the Turkish 'Derdin ne senin?' has that confrontational tone); learners may use it as a caring question. Neutral 'What's the matter?' is safer.

text: I love the sound of rain falling.

notes: Needs context (share what?); without an object it can also mean 'tell us your thoughts' (as in a group meeting) rather than using something together.

text: Don't you want to learn to drive?
Have you been here the whole time?
At the tone, please record your message.
turkish_fix: Lütfen sinyal sesinden sonra mesajınızı kaydedin.
notes: Turkish 'Sinyal sesinde' is a calque; the Turkish voicemail formula is 'sinyal sesinden sonra'.

text: Do you want me to check again?
notes: Turkish spelling error: the question particle must be written separately ('ister misin').

text: Can I have the check, please?
notes: Turkish 'Çeki' means a bank cheque, not the restaurant bill ('hesap'); 'check' is a false friend for Turkish learners.

text: I do not understand you very well.
I have to create a new site.
turkish_fix: Yeni bir web sitesi oluşturmam gerekiyor.
notes: 'site' is unclear (website or place), and Turkish 'site' usually means a housing complex; 'site yaratmak' is a calque ('oluşturmak/kurmak').

text: The room didn't have a single window.
turkish_fix: Odada tek bir pencere bile yoktu.
notes: Turkish 'Odanın bir tek penceresi yoktu' lacks 'bile' and can read 'the only thing missing was a window'.
Stiff, proverb-like; the natural saying is 'Think before you speak'.

text: We want to offer you the job.
I've decided to accept the job offer.
The number of working women is increasing.

notes: 'turn on the light' refers to the lamp (a device), not 'the brightness from the sun or a lamp'.
Formal/stiff (a doctor or form might ask this); Turkish 'İyi misin?' ('Are you OK?') drops 'health', the carrier word.

text: It's going to cost around thirty dollars.
The cost of advertising has gone up.
I'm going to the center of town.
What's the best present you've ever received?

notes: Turkish 'Ben o bilgiye sahip değilim' is stilted translationese.

text: She works in the local flower shop.
These cars are the same type.
I don't think I passed the test.

notes: Stock banter phrase ('you're an easy target'); needs context. Turkish 'Bunu çok kolay yapıyorsun' means 'you do this very easily'.
Odd habitual present with 'the day'; 'I spend all day talking' or past 'spent' is more natural.

text: We provided them with money and clothes.
I like the sound of children laughing.
That sounds too good to be true.
turkish_fix: Kulağa gerçek olamayacak kadar iyi geliyor.
notes: Turkish 'görünüyor' means 'looks', losing the hearing sense of the carrier verb 'sound'.

text: It is a nice view from here.
notes: Turkish 'O, buradan güzel bir manzara.' is an unnatural calque of 'It is'.

text: We have a bit of time now.
Look at the mountains covered with snow.
notes: First Turkish translation is ungrammatical ('Karlı kaplı' should be 'Karla kaplı').
News-style and incomplete without context (taking action about what?).
'pretty name' means pleasant-sounding, not 'nice to look at' as glossed.

text: I'm going to do that pretty soon.
notes: Turkish 'çok yakında' means 'very soon', mistranslating the carrier 'pretty' (quite, fairly).

text: There's too much money in these accounts.
notes: Odd out of context: 'too much money' in accounts suggests something suspicious; needs context.
Turkish 'böl' means 'divide'; the carrier 'cut' should be 'kes'.

text: Did you go to the market yesterday?
notes: Turkish 'market' is a false friend (grocery store), and US 'the market' can also mean a supermarket; the glossed sense is 'pazar'.

text: The chair is too low for me.
The air around here isn't very good.
notes: Turkish 'hava' here reads as 'weather'; the sentence is about air quality.

text: I'm probably never going to do that.
It's going to be a great experience.
I don't think that that's even possible.
notes: Grammatical but awkward double 'that'; natives say 'I don't think that's even possible'.

text: Don't even consider giving him the money.

notes: 'Görüşmek üzere' is idiomatic but drops the carrier 'soon'; 'Yakında görüşürüz' keeps it.
Turkish 'Resminiz' means 'your picture', not 'the picture'.
Nothing marks 'site' as a website (could be a place or building site; Turkish 'site' also means a housing complex).
Turkish 'O,' reads as 'he/she', changing the subject; 'that' refers to an explanation.

text: Pick a name from this list.
Do I have to stand in line?

notes: 'at the moment' is a fixed phrase meaning 'currently', not 'a very short period of time'.

text: I want to make that very clear.
turkish_fix: Bunu çok açık bir şekilde belirtmek istiyorum.
notes: Turkish 'Onu çok açık yapmak istiyorum' is an unnatural calque.

text: Do you think I have a chance?
I've got to go to the police.
I don't have to decide that now.
Am I still on the right road?
When are we going to land?
notes: Turkish 'karaya çıkmak' means going ashore from a ship; a plane landing is 'iniş yapmak'.

text: The teacher writes on the board.

notes: 'on sale' means discounted (US) but 'available to buy' (UK); Turkish is present tense while English is past.
Turkish 'Ailem' means 'my family'; the carrier 'parents' is 'annem babam'.

text: I'm saving money for a car.
Let's meet in front of the station.
notes: 'in front of' is a compound preposition (önünde), not the noun 'front' (the forward-facing part).

text: Do you have any interest in sports?
I wish you and your family well.
notes: 'wish someone well' is the good-wishes sense, not 'want something that may not happen'; Turkish 'iyilik diliyorum' is unidiomatic.

text: He gave his children a good education.

notes: Transitive 'grow rice' means cultivate, not the glossed 'become bigger'.

text: We had a long period of good weather.
turkish_fix: Uzun bir süre havalar güzel gitti.
notes: Turkish 'Biz uzun süre güzel hava yaşadık' is an unnatural collocation.

text: Does this medicine have any side effects?
I have to pay this bill today.
Our country produces a lot of sugar.

notes: Odd without context (implies the meat was thrown to the dog).

text: I've been there a couple of times.
I have to park my car here.
Would you like to do that instead?
turkish_fix: Bunun yerine onu yapmak ister misin?
notes: Turkish 'Yerine' without 'bunun' is unnatural.
'playing cards' here means card games (iskambil), not the glossed thick-paper/bank-card sense.
Sounds non-native; natives say 'I'd like some coffee' or 'I'd like a coffee'.
'have a drink' usually implies alcohol, not the general 'liquid for drinking'; Turkish 'içki' fixes that reading. Neutral: 'Bir şeyler içmeye gidelim'.

text: I hate doing this kind of stuff.

notes: Turkish ends with a period instead of a question mark.
'I guess' here means 'I suppose', not 'give an answer without knowing for sure'.

text: Don't be afraid to raise your hand.
notes: Turkish 'El kaldırmak' can also mean raising a hand against someone (to hit); 'Elini kaldırmak' is clear.
Turkish 'Onun ... olduğunu' reads as 'he/she is'; the English is about a thing.

text: We liked the food, especially the fish.
I don't have time to explain it.
I don't want to throw that away.
notes: Phrasal verb 'throw away' means discard, not 'send through the air with your hand'.

text: He made me sing on the stage.
Are you suggesting that I'm too young?
turkish_fix: Çok genç olduğumu mu ima ediyorsun?
notes: 'suggesting' here means implying, not 'give an idea to consider'; learners may read it as 'propose'. Turkish 'ileri sürmek' (to claim) is stiff.

text: I don't think you understand the situation.
I don't have a middle name.
I'm in the middle of something here.
notes: Idiom 'in the middle of something' means busy, not 'the central part'; Turkish is a literal calque.

text: You have to make the right choice.
I'm going to apply for that job.
Pull the door, don't push it.
He is certain to win the game.
notes: 'certain to win' means he will definitely win, not that he feels sure; learners may read it as 'he is sure he'll win'.

text: I wonder when the party's going to start.
I've got stuff I want to do.
notes: Turkish is missing the final period.

text: Thank you for your time and effort.
What exactly are you going to do?
I usually get up at seven.
The quality of rice is going down.
notes: News-like and odd without context; 'the rice' would be more natural.

text: I didn't realize you were already here.
You're the first person to mention that.
notes: Turkish 'söz edecek' (future) means 'who will mention'; should be 'bahseden'.

text: I didn't expect to see you here.
notes: Turkish 'ummadım' leans to 'didn't hope'; the natural rendering of 'expect' is 'beklemiyordum'.

text: She runs every day to stay fit.
I didn't even notice you were there.
She sent me a funny text message.
notes: 'text' appears only as a modifier in 'text message'; the glossed noun ('a text') is not used on its own.

text: Text me when you get back home.
I had an opportunity to do that.
What's the best way to contact you?
Perhaps you would like to go first.
It is ten degrees below zero now.
I don't need to know the details.
She drew a straight line on the paper.
What's your purpose for being here today?
notes: Stilted ('What brings you here today?' is natural); Turkish 'burada olmak için amacın' is an unnatural calque.

text: You're going to have to be quick.
notes: Turkish 'Hızlı olmak zorunda olacaksın' is an unnatural calque.
Turkish 'genç çocuklar' suggests teenagers; 'young children' is 'küçük çocuklar'.
Turkish 'Onun adil olduğunu' reads as 'that he/she is fair'; 'Bunun' refers to the situation.

text: Let's go ahead and do it now.
notes: Phrasal verb 'go ahead' means proceed, not 'in front; forward'; Turkish 'Devam edelim' (let's continue) is a calque.

text: I certainly don't see it that way.
I've got a little extra time right now.
I'd like to see that ring, please.

notes: Turkish 'Kopyan' means 'your copy', and 'kopya' can suggest a cheat sheet.

text: I let my friend copy my homework.
I have things I need to do.

notes: First translation uses 'bu' (= this man); 'that man' is 'o/şu adam'.
Odd, translated-sounding request; natives would more likely say 'Can I see your cat?' or 'Show me your kitten.'

text: My father works for a power company.
notes: Stilted Turkish for an everyday sentence: formal '-mektedir' and calque 'için çalışmak'; 'power company' is 'elektrik şirketi'.

text: The second lesson is very easy.
There are sixty seconds in a minute.

notes: 'Şimdi o benim sıram' is unnatural Turkish ('o' copies English 'it').

text: I can see the top of the mountain.

notes: 'An early lunch' means earlier than usual, not 'near the beginning of a period' as in 'early morning'.

text: The room is full of people.
He is very kind, just like you.
I want you to follow me.
He and I share a room.
notes: Translationese Turkish: 'O ve ben ... bir odayı' sounds unnatural.

text: I have to create a new website.

notes: Odd without context; 'see the light' is also an idiom (= finally understand), as the second Tatoeba translation 'Anlayabiliyorum' shows.

text: Now is the time for action.
notes: Rhetorical slogan from speeches and campaigns, not everyday speech.

text: I'd like to open an account.
She goes to the market once a week.
I didn't know that it was possible.
This is an excellent site for learning French.

notes: 'Bir dakika' is idiomatic but renders 'moment' as 'dakika' (minute), so it would cue 'minute'.

text: There's a big sale at the shop today.
Do you want to sit in the front?
I wish you a happy birthday.
Where can I catch a bus?
Can I have a cold drink, please?
Don't throw a stone at the dog.
The car stopped in the middle of the road.
notes: 'İstop etti' is a nonstandard colloquial spelling and suggests the engine stalled; 'stopped' is 'durdu'.

text: I'm certain that you can do that.
These products are of the same quality.

notes: 'Metin' is a written text or passage, not a phone message ('mesaj').

text: What's the purpose of your visit?
Go straight ahead and follow the signs.
They live in a little house.
He usually feels sleepy in the early afternoon.
turkish_fix: Öğleden sonranın erken saatlerinde genelde uykusu gelir.
notes: Turkish 'Öğlen erken saatlerde' is unnatural (no genitive link) and turns 'afternoon' into 'noon' (öğlen); early afternoon is 'öğleden sonranın erken saatleri'.

text: I'm very sorry for my actions.
notes: Turkish 'Eylemlerim' is translationese in an apology (eylem reads as a formal act or a protest); natural Turkish says 'yaptıklarım' (what I did), which also matches the gloss, and apologises with 'özür dilerim'.

text: Can I have the check, please?
notes: Turkish 'Çeki' means a bank cheque, not the restaurant bill ('hesap'); 'check' is a false friend for Turkish learners.
override: The English is clear and 'check' is the glossed restaurant bill; the risk is the Turkish false friend 'çek', which S5 fixes with turkish_fix.
